en: In this place, the Great Hero should dig a pit knee-deep; or rather, one should dig it in the shape of a pond, measuring one cubit on all sides. [3.1]
In the locations of the lords, one should likewise fashion a circle measuring one span;
with a concentrated mind, one should smear it all around with clay and cow dung.
Then, having filled it with water, one should cast into it a living fish.
Then, having offered the *śītalikā* oblation, one should examine the water there.
Having gone a full hundred paces and returned again, one should look once more;
the ground where the water remains steady is auspicious, while the mantra-practitioner should avoid that which is empty.
The *riktā* [tithi] would be undesirable; with noise, it brings fear to the *nāgas*.
Having taken a live fish and given it a sprig from a milky tree,
one should fill the pit with that earth or with other earth;
by this variation in form, one examines the soil.
A wise person should perform the rite of staking with pegs made of copper, iron, stone, khadira wood, or clay, or even by means of the mantra alone.
One should likewise prepare ten sharp-pointed stakes, shaped like vajras at their upper ends.
Having placed eight sugata-fingers in shape, wrapped with red thread and smeared with red sandalwood paste, in the northeast corner,
one intent on warding off obstacles should offer incense, bali-offerings, and so forth.
Then the preceptor, having risen again and being accompanied by wise disciples,
should properly delineate the mandala according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures.
Then, standing upon the central seat, he should meditate in the proper sequence.
One should visualize Mount Meru there, formed by the evolution of the four elements. In its center, one should imagine the syllable HŪṂ and from that, a vajra.
Having beheld the syllable BHRŪṂ situated there, one should [visualize] a stūpa, which is an ocean of Jinas.

Then, having reflected, one established in meditative absorption should again prepare a mandala with fragrances and perform worship to the Three Jewels and others with the five types of offerings and so forth.
The wise practitioner should offer a bali-oblation to the guardians of the directions according to his means.
Then the preceptor, joined with the bell and vajra and with palms pressed together,
having knelt down, should speak thus with a concentrated mind: [3.14]
I make this request for the sake of the stages to those established within the triple world—
those who dwell upon the stages of the triple world, the highly worthy ones.
[3.15] Who are the great lords who dwell as protectors within this triple world?
The gods, nāgas, gandharvas, daityas, kinnaras, and others—
[he established them] upon that portion of the earth esteemed as auspicious for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings. [3.16]
Furthermore, for the sake of the splendor of monasteries and the like, as well as for hearing, reflection, and so forth,
may these always lead you toward the realization of the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā). [3.17]
Still, though corrupted, I am intent on establishing my own reputation by dwelling in the future and so forth; this must be forgiven by you and others, for I shall not act otherwise. [3.18]
Having recited this with diligence, the mantra-practitioner, intent on auspiciousness, should then entreat the Earth: "O beautiful one, grant your favor.
He should likewise entreat her for food.
Oṃ jruṃ jruṃ hūṃ svāhā.
O Goddess, you are the witness to all the Buddhas, the protectors, regarding the excellence of the conduct and the methods, as well as the stages and the perfections.
Just as the forces of Māra were broken by the supreme ones, such as the Lion of the Śākyas; [3.20]
Thus, having conquered the host of Māra for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings,
I perform auspicious deeds for the purpose of engaging in all accomplishments. Having visualized the earth and its entire physical extent three times before the Master, [he says:]
Then, having given permission, she who was half-bodied, yellow, her limbs adorned with fine garments, and endowed with a triple-crested maṇḍala, remained right there in the form of the earth. [3.22]
Having obtained the mother's permission,
he should then perform [the rite] on another day, even in the forenoon, when an auspicious moment has arisen.
Furthermore, for the sake of crushing obstacles, the mantra-practitioner who has exerted effort in mantras,
assuming the majestic display of Vajrasattva and adopting the two-legged *ālīḍha* stance,
should emanate the ten wrathful deities and cause them to dwell within his own body. [3.23–24]
Whom should one establish?
Yamāntaka on the right arm, Prajñāntaka at the base of the left;
Hayagrīva on the face, and Amṛtakuṇḍalin on the secret place. [3.25]
Kuṇḍalin is in the southern part, and Ṭakkirāja is on the left;
[and] Acala is...?
Then the wise one should assign Nīladaṇḍa to the right knee;
Mahābala to the left knee; and one should visualize Sumbharāja placed upon the two ends of the feet, with Uṣṇīṣavartin on the head. [3.26–3.27]
Having thus armored himself, he should crush the leaders of obstacles;
having uttered the *ālikāli* [mantra] five times with the *kamalāvarta* [mudrā].
One should recite this verse, which is impelled by all the Buddhas: In this regard,
the verse is as follows:
"May those who are the lords of this place depart!
O gods, yakṣas, and so forth, as well as gandharvas, go away immediately!
Taking the form of obstacles, with the sound 'maṭkāra' and eyes like the sun and moon... [3.29]

One should visualize a *viśvavajra* (double-pronged vajra) at both feet, born from the syllable *hūṃ*. Having fashioned the "vajra-vision" through this method— where the left eye is made into a moon by the syllable *ṭa*, the right eye is placed upon a sun by the syllable *a*, and the fire of the eon is made into a star by the syllable *hūṃ*— [one proceeds].
Oṃ pādākarṣaṇavajra hūṃ.
Having looked out in all directions as far as the subterranean realm (pātāla), one should purify it;
holding a kīlaka at the neck with the left hand and a mallet in the right hand.
One should strike the ritual stakes with a mallet while making a loud sound:
OṂ HANA 2 SARVADUṢṬAPRADUṢṬĀN MĀRAYA 2 KĪLAYA 2 SARVAPĀPĀN PHAṬ | OṂ GHA GHA GHĀṬAYA 2 SARVADUṢṬĀN PHAṬ KĪLAYA 2 SARVAPĀPĀN PHAṬ |

Oṃ āḥ hūṃ! Yamāntakṛt, nail down all evil Indras and Upendras together with their retinues! Hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ āḥ hūṃ! Prajñāntakṛt, nail down all evil Yamas together with their retinues! Hūṃ phaṭ! [The mantras for the east and south are missing.]
In the west: Oṃ āḥ hūṃ! Padmāntakṛt, nail down Varuṇa and his retinue! Hūṃ phaṭ! In the north:

Oṃ āḥ hūṃ! Vighnāntakṛt, nail-pierce all the wicked Kuberas and Gaṇapatis together with their retinues! Hūṃ phaṭ! [In the southeast. Oṃ āḥ hūṃ! Ṭakkirāja, nail-pierce all the wicked Agnis together with their retinues! Hūṃ phaṭ!
In the southwest:
Oṃ āḥ hūṃ! Nīladaṇḍa, nail down all the wicked Nairṛtis together with their retinues! Hūṃ phaṭ! Then, in the northwest:
Oṃ āḥ hūṃ! Mahābala, nail down all malevolent winds together with their retinues! Hūṃ phaṭ! [In the northeast.
Oṃ āḥ hūṃ! Acala, nail down all malevolent Īśānas together with their retinues! Hūṃ phaṭ!
Then again, toward the east:
Oṃ āḥ bhrūṃ hūṃ! Nail down Uṣṇīṣacakravartin, together with all the wicked Moon, Sun, and Pitāmaha, along with their retinues! Hūṃ phaṭ!
Then, having gone to the west:
Tato oṃ āḥ hūṃ! O Sumbharāja, together with the earth-deity and your retinue, nail them down! Hūṃ phaṭ!
Having meditated upon the act of nailing [them down], one whose nature is compassion ensures that there are no obstacles.
Then, one should again meditate in the center:
Oṃ bhrūṃ haḥ hrīḥ pratīccha bhūr bhuvaḥ svāhā.
Having first presented the forms of the flowers of the factors of enlightenment,
one should offer water in due order with the victory-flasks and the others.
Then, with palms joined in reverence, one should say to the Protectors for the sake of their arrangement:
May the Buddhas, the compassionate lords of the world, attend to me;
as well as the Arhats and Bodhisattvas, and whoever among the beings possesses great supernatural power, all who delight in the teaching and possess the vajra-eye.
I, the Vajrī named so-and-so, for the sake of the Three Jewels, shall construct a monastery and other such works for the donor according to his name. [3.37]
Out of compassion for me and my disciples,
you all ought to be present at this offering of the guest-water (argha). [3.38]
Having raised a clamor of musical instruments and having worshipped the world with sandalwood known as *pūgamālā*, one should perform the rite of dismissal after circumambulating. || 3.39 ||

The sequence of their value is stated according to tradition for those made of wood, clay, or painted on canvas, as well as for those fashioned from stone, gold, and so forth, whether cast or wrought. [3.40]
"The Tathāgata has whatever intrinsic nature, this world has that same intrinsic nature;
the Tathāgata is without intrinsic nature, this world is without intrinsic nature"—from such firm conviction. [3.41]

Having again generated the deity through the yoga of Vajrasattva and so forth, by means of the sixfold sequence beginning with the moon and vajra, and by way of the distinctions of the five gnoses and so forth,
one should place within the heart of each [deity] its respective seed-syllable.
Alternatively, one should place the three syllables there, distributed across the three locations. One should cause the deity to descend into clay, stone, wood, and so forth.
One should illuminate the recitation and so forth with the verses beginning with "tatsaṃnihita" and so on.

For the sake of purifying the hands of the artisans, one should especially empower them at the heart, throat, and head by means of the three principles (*tritattva*) through the application of the Moon and Vajra. [3.44–45]

Having consecrated the belly and other parts seven times with Vajrasattva, one should personally take the food, the brush, and so forth, and offer them in accordance with the conduct of a sentient being. [3.46]
Having recited the hundred-syllable mantra, one should indeed perform the dismissal once more;

[one should offer] cattle, grain, buffaloes, and so forth, as well as other gifts to the preceptor. [3.47] Regarding "other [gifts] to the preceptor" in the verse on food: [it refers to] other [items].
One should also give to a skilled artisan according to one's ability and in a fitting manner;
then, having provided a communal meal for the Saṅgha, one should organize a gathering of virtuous people.
One whose nature is compassion should dedicate the merit toward awakening as it truly is; for the sake of delivering sentient beings, one should perform the entire rite of dismissal. [3.49]
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for the common offering of monasteries, groves, cloths, and books.
